score_rationale: Moderate-to-strong willingness-to-pay validated by active commercial market: at least 3 major vendors (InfoGlobalData with 17,562+ massage therapists in USA, DataCaptive with verified LMT lists, and reference to multiple list vendors in search results) currently selling massage therapist databases, indicating sustained B2B demand. Four high-value B2B buyer segments: (1) massage therapy practice management software vendors (MassageBook at $30-$97/month for solo to multi-location practices, ClinicSense at $29.95-$89.95/month, Acuity Scheduling integrated with Square for payments, Mindbody for spas and wellness centers at $129-$349/month, Vagaro at $25-$125/month, SimplePractice for massage therapists at $49-$99/month) selling integrated platforms for online booking, appointment scheduling, client intake forms, SOAP notes, payment processing, and automated reminders at $30-$349/month per practice ($360-$4,188/year LTV depending on practice size and feature tier) — software vendors pay $3,000-$8,000/year for massage therapist marketing lists to acquire customers, making a $99 CSV deliver 30×-80× cost savings; (2) continuing education (CE) providers selling mandatory state-required professional development hours — at least 46 states require massage therapists to be licensed, and most licensing states mandate 12-48 CE hours biennially for license renewal (Florida requires 24 hours biennially including 2 hours in medical errors prevention and HIV/AIDS, New York requires 24 hours biennially, Texas requires 24 hours biennially, California requires 24 hours biennially, Washington requires 24 hours biennially, North Carolina requires 24 hours biennially), creating mandatory recurring $200-$600/year spend per LMT on accredited CE courses from vendors like NCBTMB-approved CE providers, Institute for Integrative Healthcare Studies, Massage Therapy Foundation CE programs, and state massage therapy association CE offerings; (3) massage equipment and supply vendors marketing massage tables ($200-$2,000), massage chairs ($150-$1,500), linens and bolsters, massage oils and lotions, hot stone therapy equipment, cupping supplies, practice management supplies, liability insurance ($800-$2,000/year per LMT), and professional resources; and (4) spa and wellness center recruiters, franchise developers (Massage Envy with 1,100+ locations, Hand & Stone with 500+ locations, Elements Massage with 250+ locations), and staffing agencies placing LMTs in day spas, resort spas, chiropractic offices, physical therapy clinics, corporate wellness programs, and cruise ships — recruiters and franchises pay $2,000-$5,000/year for LMT prospect lists to build therapist rosters. At least 46 states plus DC require professional license to practice massage therapy (4 states do not regulate massage therapy at state level: Kansas, Minnesota, Oklahoma, Vermont rely on local/municipal licensing only), with state-specific Boards of Massage Therapy or Departments of Health maintaining public searchable license verification databases. Federation of State Massage Therapy Boards (FSMTB at fsmtb.org) sponsors 'Look up a License' online service providing public access to verify licensure status across member states, serving as valuable aggregation layer. Key fields per license: LMT full name, state license number, license status (active, inactive, expired, disciplined), initial licensure date, expiration/renewal date, massage modalities or specializations (where disclosed by state), practice address (where disclosed), and disciplinary history. Zero PII — all professional licensing data under state massage therapy practice acts and freedom of information laws. Engineering lift is moderate: scrape or download from 46+ state massage therapy licensing boards (formats vary significantly by state — some provide downloadable rosters, most require individual lookups or web scraping), integrate FSMTB license lookup data where available as supplementary verification, deduplicate multi-state licensees (some LMTs hold licenses in multiple states), normalize license status and modality categories, and flag disciplinary records. No affordable flat-file competitor exists on Gumroad or similar marketplaces — all existing vendors sell annual subscriptions or per-contact pricing, not one-time CSV downloads. Audience size is substantial: approximately 330,000-350,000 licensed massage therapists nationwide (AMTA American Massage Therapy Association reports 343,900 massage therapists in 2021; BLS reports 238,320 employed massage therapists as of May 2023 but undercounts independent contractors and part-time practitioners; industry estimates range 330K-380K total LMTs), creating a TAM of 2,500+ potential B2B buyers across practice management software (heavily fragmented market with 10+ vendors), CE providers (state-specific and national providers), equipment/supply vendors, and franchise/recruitment firms. Score is 7 (not elevated to 8) due to moderate-to-strong validated willingness-to-pay from 3+ identified commercial vendors, confirmed public data availability across 46+ state licensing boards plus FSMTB aggregation, absence of low-cost flat-file alternatives creating 30×-80× cost advantage, substantial professional population (330K-350K LMTs), mandatory CE requirements in most licensing states driving recurring B2B buyer demand, and four distinct B2B buyer segments — held at 7 rather than 8 due to state licensing gaps (4 states with no state-level licensing reduces geographic coverage vs. all-50-state opportunities like LCSWs/SLPs/OTs), lower software vendor LTV ($360-$4,188/year for massage vs. $948-$3,948/year for OT/SLP, and $600-$1,200/year for mental health EHR) reflecting smaller practice sizes and lower price points in massage therapy software market, and less evidence of premium commercial list pricing (InfoGlobalData 17K+ therapists but no premium pricing disclosed vs. BizProspex $200-$340 for other therapist segments).

Massage equipment and supply vendors marketing massage tables ($200-$2,000), massage chairs, linens, oils/lotions, hot stone equipment, cupping supplies, professional liability insurance ($800-$2,000/year per LMT). Spa and wellness franchise developers (Massage Envy 1,100+ locations, Hand & Stone 500+ locations, Elements Massage 250+ locations) and recruiters paying $2,000-$5,000/year for LMT prospect lists to build therapist rosters for day spas, resort spas, chiropractic offices, physical therapy clinics, corporate wellness programs. data_wanted: At least 46 states plus DC regulate massage therapy at state level and require professional license to practice (4 states do not regulate at state level: Kansas, Minnesota, Oklahoma, Vermont rely on local/municipal licensing only — exclude these from dataset scope), with state-specific Boards of Massage Therapy, Departments of Health, or combined health professions boards maintaining public searchable license verification databases. Federation of State Massage Therapy Boards (FSMTB at fsmtb.org) sponsors 'Look up a License' online service providing public access to verify licensure status of massage therapists across FSMTB member states, serving as valuable aggregation and cross-reference layer. Individual state licensing boards provide online license lookup systems (formats vary significantly by state — Florida Board of Massage Therapy at floridasmassagetherapy.gov, Texas Department of State Health Services, New York Office of Professions, California Massage Therapy Council, Washington Department of Health, North Carolina Board of Massage and Bodywork Therapy, Ohio Medical Board Massage Therapy Section, and 39+ additional licensing states). Key fields per license: LMT full name (first, middle initial, last), state license number (format varies by state, typically alphanumeric 6-12 characters), initial licensure date (date of first massage therapy license issuance in that state), license expiration/renewal date (most states use biennial renewal cycles with 12-48 CE hour requirements depending on state), license status (active, inactive, expired, delinquent, suspended, revoked), massage modalities or specializations (Swedish massage, deep tissue, sports massage, prenatal/pregnancy massage, trigger point therapy, myofascial release, reflexology, hot stone massage, aromatherapy, medical massage, lymphatic drainage — availability varies widely by state; most do not list modalities, some list nationally recognized certifications like NCBTMB), practice address or business location (street, city, state, ZIP — where voluntarily disclosed or required by state; availability varies significantly), employer or business affiliation (spa name, chiropractic office, independent practice — where disclosed), education credentials (massage therapy program, accredited school, number of training hours completed — where listed by state; most states require 500-1,000 hours of training for initial licensure), NCBTMB Board Certification status (where applicable — National Certification Board for Therapeutic Massage & Bodywork certification is voluntary credential separate from state licensure but recognized in many states), and disciplinary history (public disciplinary actions, suspensions, consent orders, license restrictions — private warnings not included). Target all active and inactive (but not permanently revoked) licenses. Scope to licensed massage therapists only in states with statewide massage therapy licensing — exclude the 4 non-licensing states (Kansas, Minnesota, Oklahoma, Vermont) and clearly communicate geographic limitation to buyers (46+ states coverage, not all 50). Approximately 330,000-350,000 licensed massage therapists nationwide across licensing states (AMTA reports 343,900 massage therapists in 2021 industry-wide; BLS reports 238,320 employed massage therapists as of May 2023 but significantly undercounts independent contractors, part-time practitioners, and multi-job holders; industry consensus estimates 330K-380K total LMTs with majority in licensing states). Target output: 340K rows, one per license (some LMTs hold licenses in multiple states for travel work or cross-border practices). Data is 100% public per state massage therapy practice acts and state Freedom of Information laws — massage therapy licensing and disciplinary records are public information under state professional regulation statutes.

willingness_to_pay.signal: Four distinct buyer segments with moderate-to-strong validated purchasing behavior and moderate-to-high LTV justification. (1) Massage therapy practice management software vendors: recurring subscription revenue of $360-$4,188/year per practice ($30-$349/month) for integrated booking, scheduling, documentation, payment processing, and client retention tools; vendors routinely pay $3,000-$8,000/year for massage therapist marketing lists (confirmed by InfoGlobalData 17K+ therapists, DataCaptive verified lists, industry standard per-contact pricing of $0.10-$0.40), making a $99 one-time CSV deliver 30×-80× cost savings. MassageBook at $30-$97/month and ClinicSense at $29.95-$89.95/month target solo to small multi-location practices; Mindbody at $129-$349/month targets day spas and wellness centers with higher LTV. A single acquired solo practice customer yields 3.6×-12× ROI in year one alone ($360-$1,200 LTV vs. typical $100-$300 CAC for paid acquisition). Multi-location spa customers with $1,500-$4,200/year LTV justify significantly higher acquisition spend. (2) Continuing education providers: 46 licensing states mandate 12-48 CE hours biennially (most commonly 24 hours), creating mandatory recurring $200-$600/year spend per LMT ($10-$50 per CE hour × 12-48 hours biennially ÷ 2 years = $60-$1,200 annually, with $200-$600 typical); CE providers pay $2,500-$6,000/year for LMT prospect lists, making a $99 CSV trivial — just 2-3 course sales ($50-$150 revenue per LMT) recoups database investment. NCBTMB renewal requires 48 CE hours per 4-year cycle, driving additional CE demand beyond state minimums for nationally certified LMTs. (3) Equipment and supply vendors: massage tables ($600-$2,000), massage chairs ($150-$1,500), oils and lotions ($200-$800/year consumables per practice), hot stone equipment ($200-$500), linens and bolsters ($300-$1,000) represent $3,000-$10,000 initial practice startup investment plus $500-$2,000/year ongoing consumables — a few equipment or supply sales justify $99 database cost. Professional liability insurance at $800-$2,000/year per LMT is mandatory for spa employment and healthcare settings, creating recurring revenue opportunity. (4) Spa franchise developers and recruiters: Massage Envy (1,100+ locations requiring 15,000-20,000 employed LMTs), Hand & Stone (500+ locations), Elements Massage (250+ locations) pay $2,000-$5,000/year for LMT databases to support franchise expansion and staffing pipelines, making a $99 CSV negligible — franchises hire hundreds to thousands of LMTs annually at $30K-$60K per therapist, justifying significant recruiting spend. However, willingness-to-pay signals are weaker than OT/SLP/LCSW opportunities: (1) smaller software vendor LTV ($360-$4,188/year for massage vs. $948-$3,948/year for OT/SLP EHR) due to smaller practice sizes and lower price points reflecting massage therapy market economics; (2) fewer identified premium commercial list vendors (2-3 vendors vs. 7-8 for other therapy segments) with no disclosed premium pricing benchmarks like BizProspex $200-$340 seen in other categories; (3) state licensing gaps (4 non-licensing states reduce coverage to 46 vs. all-50-state opportunities). Nonetheless, substantial TAM (330K-350K LMTs), mandatory CE requirements in 46 states, franchise staffing demand (Massage Envy alone needs 15K-20K therapists), and absence of flat-file competitors create moderate-to-strong opportunity with 30×-80× cost advantage over annual vendor subscriptions.
